doc.title: Derek Brown interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, March 5, 2021

title: Musical mid-life crisis in grad school and giving up imitating Sonny Rollins
summary: A younger student outplayed him, he wanted to be Sonny Rollins, then realized he should play how he wants; musicians should be honest about what they like.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Yeah well I mean I had like a kind of musical mid-life crisis in grad school, that period where I was working really hard but kind of burning out at the same time. And it came from, I specifically remember the moment. I was second year grad school — I was a grad assistant so I was supposed to be one of the top people. I was getting paid to be in school. I was in charge of a quote unquote beginning jazz combo with some freshman in it. And in came this punk saxophone kid who played circles around me. He was twice as good as me. I was five years older. He was twice as good and it just drove me nuts. I’m sure other musicians can relate to this. It’s impossible not to compare ourselves. But it drove me nuts and I remember thinking like I’m twice his age, surely I’ve practiced more than him, does he just have something in him? And it made me think if I’m not the best one in this room, I’m not the best one at all in Cincinnati. I’m definitely far from the best — how am I going to make a name for myself out there? How am I going to get noticed? And thinking about all the internet things and what is it, why would anyone listen to me when there are people twice as good as me. And I worked so hard for this. That is so hard. Now I wish I could say that then something switched and it was like oh I’ll do BEATBoxSAX and I’ll do solo concerts and I’ll do all these extended — no of course it never works that cleanly and you go through some really dark, hard times. But that was right around the time that I got that teaching gig in Texas and so I had that time to just realize you know what? I’m going to stop just completely only trying to imitate people, because I wanted to be the next Sonny Rollins. He was my gut at that time. And I realized there’s ten thousand other sax players that want to be exactly like Sonny Rollins. And then the crazy thing is none of us will ever be exactly Sonny Rollins because, you know, he had his way of playing and he had his own life, you know, influences. We’ll never be that same way. And so it was just like once again, if I’m going to play this instrument it’s going to be exactly how I want to play it. I wasn’t even at that point thinking, dreaming so much about a performing career. I think I was probably thinking it wasn’t going to happen when I got that teaching job. I’m not saying that I was like giving up or anything, because that was a great, great gig. But it did allow me to kind of relax, like I said, and just pursue what I wanted to pursue. I don’t think I would have said that time I’m seeking my own

unique sound, it was just truly seeking what I like. And that’s another thing with that whole honestly listening to yourself. I think more musicians, or a lot of musicians, need to be honest about what they truly like in music. It’s kind of like when I was a teacher and I was teaching some of these saxophone majors, they were majors in music. They wanted to perform for a living. And like let’s say it was a classical student. And I’d say, hey have you listened to this piece? What recordings do you like? And they were like, no. And then have you listened to any classical saxophone? And it’s like they don’t listen to classical saxophone at all. Like almost never. And it’s like you’re pursuing this full time. Like this is going to be your thing, and you don’t even really like the music? You know that seems strange. Or, and that’s an extreme example, there are other people I think, they’re imitating someone because that’s who they think they’re supposed to like. Or in the typical jazz hierarchy, in the evolution of jazz, you’re supposed to start, like if you just look at Coltrane. You start with “Blue Trane” but then you move on. That’s too simple now, you move on to “Giant Steps,” really fast harmonic language. You move on to “A Love Supreme” where he opens it all up. And then you move on and you kind of don’t look back, and you kind of, you know it’s like it’s a lesser form of music. And for some people that’s great. If avante garde jazz is your thing and that’s what gets you up in the morning, go for it. That’s awesome. We need people in this world that are excited about what they’re doing. But if you’re doing that just because that’s what the other kids, the other sax players are doing, your heart’s not going to be in it and I don’t think you’re going to have what it takes to push through the highs and a lot of lows of a music career. You have to absolutely love and be obsessed with the music you’re pursuing. And that was kind of what I was getting closer to when I was coming across the music of Bobby McFerrin and Eddie Harris and that kind of idea.
